explanations.answer: They do more harm than good
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, “…your gatherings do more harm than good.” (1 Corinthians 11:17) He's not grumbling about a small thing. Church is supposed to build people up, and he says theirs is doing the opposite.

Paul never says the room is empty. He talks about when they "come together as a church" (1 Corinthians 11:18), so people are showing up. The trouble is what happens once they're all in there. A packed room can still have a problem.

explanations.answer: They always run far too long
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about how long the gatherings last. His complaint is that they do "more harm than good." (1 Corinthians 11:17) Honestly, a long meeting I could forgive. I've watched dough rise, so I know patience.
Not quite. Paul says he hears there are divisions among them, and then adds, "in part I believe it." (1 Corinthians 11:18) So he doesn't wave the report away. He takes it seriously, at least in part.

Right. The text says, "I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it." (1 Corinthians 11:18) He believes at least part of the report. He didn't throw it out.

Yes. Paul says, "…there must be differences among you to show which of you are approved." (1 Corinthians 11:19) The text puts it right there: approved. Now, I'm not going to dress up what that means beyond what Paul says.
Paul never says the differences are about who should lead. He says they show "which of you are approved." (1 Corinthians 11:19) Nobody's getting handed a clipboard here.
Paul doesn't bring up who believed first anywhere in this passage. The differences show "which of you are approved." (1 Corinthians 11:19) No stopwatch required.
Yep. Paul says, "as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal." (1 Corinthians 11:21) Everybody's looking out for their own plate. Eating together is supposed to mean, well, together.
The text says the opposite. "…each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal." (1 Corinthians 11:21) So nobody's passing the plate. Everybody's just getting theirs.
You got it. Paul asks, "Don't you have your own homes in which to eat and drink?" (1 Corinthians 11:22) It's a pointed question. If you're just filling your own plate, your kitchen table can do that.
Paul never mentions markets. He asks about their own homes. (1 Corinthians 11:22) A market is a fine place to go, but it's not what he's asking about.
Temples don't come up here. Paul asks, "Don't you have your own homes in which to eat and drink?" (1 Corinthians 11:22) He's pointing them back to their own front doors.
Right. Paul asks if they "humiliate those who have nothing." (1 Corinthians 11:22) That's the one he's thinking of. It's the person at the table with empty hands.
Paul doesn't name prophets or teachers in this question. He asks if they "humiliate those who have nothing." (1 Corinthians 11:22) Look at who's left out of the meal.
The leaders aren't named here. The people Paul asks about are "those who have nothing." (1 Corinthians 11:22) That's the ones sitting there with no meal at all.

Not this time. Paul says, "I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you." (1 Corinthians 11:23) He doesn't mention Peter, one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2). The Lord is who he names.
Right. Paul says he received it "from the Lord." (1 Corinthians 11:23) Peter, one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2), isn't named as the source. Paul points straight to the Lord.
Yes. Jesus says, "…do this in remembrance of Me." (1 Corinthians 11:24) That's His reason, right in His own words. Simple and clear.
Jesus says nothing about a harvest. His words are, "…do this in remembrance of Me." (1 Corinthians 11:24) The reason is remembering Him.
A feast isn't mentioned as the reason. Jesus says, "…do this in remembrance of Me." (1 Corinthians 11:24) The reason is to remember Him.

explanations.answer: The new covenant in My blood
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood…" (1 Corinthians 11:25) Those are His words about the cup. It's worth a slow read.
Jesus doesn't call the cup that here. He says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood…" (1 Corinthians 11:25) It's the new covenant.
Not what Jesus says. He says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood…" (1 Corinthians 11:25) Sinai doesn't come up in this passage at all.
Right. Paul says, "…you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." (1 Corinthians 11:26) Every time they eat the bread and drink the cup, they're proclaiming it. And it goes on until He comes.
Paul doesn't use that word here. He says they "proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." (1 Corinthians 11:26) The word is death.
Kingdom isn't the word in this verse. Paul says they "proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." (1 Corinthians 11:26) Death is what the bread and cup proclaim.

explanations.answer: The body and blood of the Lord
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says that person "will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord." (1 Corinthians 11:27) That's serious language. It's about the Lord's own body and blood.
Paul doesn't mention Moses, Israel's leader, or his law here. He says sinning "against the body and blood of the Lord." (1 Corinthians 11:27) That's what's at stake.
Elders don't come up in this verse. Paul says it's sinning "against the body and blood of the Lord." (1 Corinthians 11:27) The offense is against the Lord.
Right. Paul says, "Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup." (1 Corinthians 11:28) It's a look in the mirror before the table.
Paul doesn't say wash. The word is examine. (1 Corinthians 11:28) That's a check on yourself, not a trip to the sink.
Close in spirit, but it's not Paul's word. He says each one must "examine himself." (1 Corinthians 11:28) Examine is the one.
Yes. Paul says that person "eats and drinks judgment on himself." (1 Corinthians 11:29) That's the weight of the thing. Without recognizing the body, that's what's being eaten and drunk.
Not what Paul says. The text says "eats and drinks judgment on himself." (1 Corinthians 11:29) That's the opposite of a blessing.
Paul doesn't say honor. The text says "eats and drinks judgment on himself." (1 Corinthians 11:29) It's judgment.
Yes. Paul says, "Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment." (1 Corinthians 11:31) Notice the "we." He includes himself.
The text says the opposite. "Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment." (1 Corinthians 11:31) And Paul says "we," so he's including himself.

explanations.answer: So we won't be condemned with the world
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says, "…we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world." (1 Corinthians 11:32) That's the purpose he gives. It's discipline, and discipline has a goal.

explanations.answer: So we'll stop gathering together for a while
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. The discipline is "so that we will not be condemned with the world." (1 Corinthians 11:32) Nothing here about taking a break.

explanations.answer: So the whole world will fear the church
explanations.explanation: Not what the text says. The discipline is "so that we will not be condemned with the world." (1 Corinthians 11:32) It's about us, not about scaring anybody.
Yes. Paul says, "…when you come together to eat, wait for one another." (1 Corinthians 11:33) Plain and simple. Nobody digs in until everybody's there.
Paul doesn't tell them to split up. He says, "…wait for one another." (1 Corinthians 11:33) They're meant to eat together.
Paul doesn't say that. His words are, "…wait for one another." (1 Corinthians 11:33) Nobody's first in line.

explanations.answer: So coming together won't result in judgment
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says, "If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you come together it will not result in judgment." (1 Corinthians 11:34) That's his reason, in his words.

explanations.answer: So the elders can always eat first
explanations.explanation: Elders aren't mentioned here. Paul says it's "so that when you come together it will not result in judgment." (1 Corinthians 11:34) That's the purpose.

explanations.answer: So the gatherings can end much sooner
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't talk about how quickly the gatherings end. He says it's "so that when you come together it will not result in judgment." (1 Corinthians 11:34) Nobody's watching the clock.
